stops.title: The question
stops.text: SVDQuant asks a sharp question. How can a twelve billion parameter diffusion transformer like FLUX.1 be made genuinely faster, not just smaller? The authors argue it takes four bit weights and four bit activations, which people write as W four A four. Nobody had made that work on big diffusion models. Their answer ends up 3.6 times smaller and about three times faster than weight-only four bit. For the LTX-2.3 study, the interesting part is how they handle outliers, even though the speed part will not transfer to OpenVINO.

stops.title: The whole idea in one picture
stops.text: Here is the whole method in one picture. First, smoothing divides the activations by a per-channel factor, which pushes their outliers into the weights. Then a small sixteen bit low-rank branch, two thin matrices from a singular value decomposition, takes over those weight outliers. What is left is a flat residual. That residual is quantized to four bits and multiplied with the four bit activations. So the outliers are never rounded at all. They live in a tiny high-precision side path.

stops.title: Why four bits is hard
stops.text: Why go to all this trouble? Look at the left side. Four bit numbers offer only sixteen levels, and a single outlier sets the range, so most values land in just one or two levels. Now the right side. Weight-only four bit saves memory, but the weights are upcast and the multiply still runs in sixteen bits. Diffusion models are compute-bound, so that brings no speed-up. Real speed needs both operands in four bits, and then both must survive the outlier problem.

stops.title: The offline recipe
stops.text: This is the recipe, and it runs once per layer, offline. A small set of COCO prompts gives calibration activations. For each layer they search the smoothing strength alpha by output error, smooth the weight, and keep the top thirty-two or so singular directions as the sixteen bit branch. The residual is then quantized with GPTQ, the method covered earlier. Optionally they repeat the split on what quantization left behind and keep the best. Notice there is no retraining anywhere.

stops.title: Move the problem, then remove it
stops.text: This figure holds the intuition most worth remembering. On the left, both activations and weights have outlier channels, so both are hard. In the middle, smoothing makes the activations easy, but the weight outliers grow bigger. Smoothing alone only moves the problem. On the right, the low-rank branch soaks up the dominant part of the weight, and the residual becomes tiny and flat. This works because smoothing makes the weight strongly low-rank, with a few huge singular values and a flat tail.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: Does it work? Lower LPIPS means closer to the full-precision image. On FLUX dev, both four bit SVDQuant variants beat NF4 weight-only quantization, which is not even faster. On PixArt Sigma the contrast is sharper. ViDiT-Q at W four A four collapses to an LPIPS of 0.854. SVDQuant at the same setting reaches 0.323, better even than ViDiT-Q with eight bit activations. So the low-rank branch is what finally makes full four bit quantization usable.

stops.title: What it costs
stops.text: Now the cost, which matters most for this project. On the left, the ablation: the low-rank branch gives the biggest quality gain, and GPTQ adds a little more on top. On the right, latency per step on a 4090. Run naively, the extra branch adds about eighteen percent, 250 against 212 milliseconds, because it rereads the input and writes a large output. Their fused engine, Nunchaku, brings it back to 218. OpenVINO has no such fused kernel, so expect the unfused number.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what does the thesis take from it? The four bit activation speed-up does not carry over, because OpenVINO has no four bit activation multiply, and Arc accelerates int8, not int4. But every piece of the layer is a standard operation, so it exports without custom ops. Use SVDQuant as a quality tool: smooth and split each layer in PyTorch, keep the branch in sixteen bits, compress only the residual with NNCF, and benchmark the overhead on long video token sequences. Next, DVD-Quant brings us back to video diffusion transformers.
